findings.title: Async rendering converts action failure into successful output
findings.trigger: Jinja compilation or asynchronous rendering raises, including sandbox SecurityError, range OverflowError, or loader TypeError.
findings.observedBehavior: The renderer logs and returns an error message as an ordinary string; gather returns normally and the action lifecycle sees no ActionFailed.
findings.impact: An automation can be recorded as succeeded and deduplicated even though its user template did not render and the action used error text as payload.
findings.recommendation: Raise a typed render exception and translate it at the action boundary into ActionFailed while retaining template error details.

evidence.description: The exception branch returns formatted failure text instead of propagating failure.
Only ActionFailed selects the failure lifecycle branch.
A normal return records the action as successful.
The snapshot test codifies returned error text for a render failure.

findings.title: Sync rendering makes a runtime template error look like a hydrated value
findings.trigger: A template passes static syntax and loop validation but raises while the synchronous Jinja renderer evaluates it.
findings.observedBehavior: The renderer returns failure text, and jinja_handler returns that text directly instead of an InvalidJinja placeholder.
findings.impact: Hydration consumers receive a string that looks like a rendered parameter, so raise-on-error and placeholder handling cannot identify the invalid template.
findings.recommendation: Raise a typed render exception and have jinja_handler translate it into InvalidJinja so the existing hydration error contract applies.

evidence.description: The synchronous exception branch returns formatted failure text.
Only validation-time syntax and security exceptions become InvalidJinja.
Runtime renderer output is returned without an error translation step.

findings.title: Docker pull can return a stale cached image after a streamed error
findings.trigger: The Docker daemon yields an error object in the low-level pull stream while a matching image tag already exists locally.
findings.observedBehavior: The worker uses docker-py's high-level pull, which consumes each stream record without inspecting error fields and then gets the local image by tag.
findings.impact: An always-pull or freshness-sensitive run may start a container from stale local content while logging that it pulled the requested image.
findings.recommendation: Consume the low-level decoded pull stream, raise on an error record, and fetch the image only after the stream completes successfully.

evidence.description: The dependency iterates every pull stream record.
The loop body explicitly does nothing with those records.
Container creation continues after the high-level pull returns.
The retained test mocks only high-level pull invocation, not streamed error behavior.

findings.title: Deserialization failure prevents the Prefect completion callback
findings.trigger: The wrapped process future raises or returns bytes that cloudpickle cannot deserialize inside the adapter callback.
findings.observedBehavior: The adapter raises before invoking its supplied callback; concurrent.futures logs that callback exception, while Prefect's completion event is never set.
findings.impact: as_completed and callback-driven flow bookkeeping can wait forever or leave the flow run as a zombie even though the process future is done.
findings.recommendation: Store the adapter error as future state, invoke the consumer callback with the wrapper future in all outcomes, and expose the error from result and exception.

evidence.description: Deserialization occurs before the supplied completion callback.
The supported runtime catches ordinary callback exceptions.
as_completed blocks on an event set only by its callback.
Process-pool results are wrapped in this adapter before Prefect observes them.

findings.title: Task concurrency cleanup reports success while a slot remains held
findings.trigger: Reading, decrementing, or revoking an acquired V2 task-concurrency lease raises while a rule fizzles after acquisition.
findings.observedBehavior: cleanup logs the exception and returns, so the orchestration rule context exits without exposing that its acquisition side effects were not reverted.
findings.impact: The concurrency limit retains an active slot or lease and can unnecessarily block later task runs until independent recovery occurs.
findings.recommendation: Propagate cleanup failure from the rule lifecycle and centralize release so decrement success and lease revocation are checked consistently.

evidence.description: Cleanup is responsible for decrementing the acquired V2 slot.
Every release exception enters a logging-only branch.
The rule lifecycle awaits cleanup to revert fizzle side effects.
The retained integration test establishes that abort cleanup owns V2 lease release.

rejectedLookalikes.reason: General event delivery is explicitly optional and returns None, while the semantically required EventTooLarge validation error is re-raised separately.
Anonymous SDK telemetry is documented as fire-and-forget and the boolean return preserves delivery status without changing workflow success.
This cross-platform capability probe supplies a documented conservative numeric default when either resource or ctypes probing is unavailable.

unresolvedBoundaries.reason: This logging-only flow lease cleanup resembles the task defect, but retained comments and lifecycle behavior imply lease-reaper recovery and do not establish the duration or externally promised cleanup result.
unresolvedBoundaries.recommendedNextStep: Inject decrement and revoke failures in a flow-concurrency integration test and observe slot availability, lease metadata, retry behavior, and reaper timing.
